etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English growen, from Old English grōwan (“to grow, increase, flourish, germinate”), from Proto-West Germanic *grōan, from Proto-Germanic *grōaną (“to grow, grow green”), from Proto-Indo-European *gʰreh₁- (“to grow, become green”).

definitions.definition: (ergative) To become larger, to increase in magnitude.

quote.citation: 1960 December, “Talking of trains: B.R. safety in 1959”, in Trains Illustrated, page 708:
quote.text: [...] but the dangers to trespassers, especially children, are growing, and a vigorous educational programme is urged.

definitions.definition: (ergative, of plants) To undergo growth; to be present (somewhere)
(transitive) To cause or allow something to become bigger, especially to cultivate plants.

quote.citation: 2011 March 1, Peter Roff, “Another Foolish Move By Congress”, in Fox News‎[1]:
quote.text: The Bush administration – which sought to grow the number of fisheries managed under a program known as “catch shares”...

quote.citation: 2023 July 10, James Poniewozik, “The Twitter Watch Party Is Over”, in The New York Times‎[2]:
quote.text: And — again to overgeneralize from my experience — users may not want a second Twitter either. I was a heavy Twitter user for over a decade. I loved it until I didn’t. I made connections, grew a following, floated ideas, had fun. But it also became a second, often angry, voice inside my head. Do I want to replace it with another one?

definitions.definition: (copulative) To assume a condition or quality over time.

quote.citation: 1967, Barbara Sleigh, Jessamy, Sevenoaks, Kent: Bloomsbury, published 1993, →ISBN, page 18:
quote.text: In fact she was so bus doing all the things that anyone might, who finds themselves alone in an empty house, that she did not notice at first when it began to turn dusk and the rooms to grow dim.

definitions.definition: (intransitive, obsolete) To become attached or fixed; to adhere.

quote.citation: 1595 December 9 (first known performance), William Shakespeare, “The life and death of King Richard the Second”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies: Published According to the True Originall Copies (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act V, scene iii]:
quote.text: Our knees shall kneel till to the ground they grow.
